Forward to nature: Ecological subjectivity after the discursive turn

Benjamin Glasson

Benjamin Glasson

Australia

Benjamin Glasson   About the Author Benjamin Glasson teaches in the School of Social and Political Sciences at the University of Melbourne. His research investigates the discursive strategies by which appeals to ethical and epistemic authority are made in fields marked by uncertainty and complexity. aglasson@unimelb.edu.au
ecology, Lacan, Laclau and Mouffe, master-signifier, dislocation

Contemporary environmental politics is generally dominated by two discourses: scepticism/denialism and liberal, managerialist reformism. Romantic-inspired environmentalism and deep ecology, on the other hand, promote the notion of an ecological subject as the key to unlocking this double bind. Yet theoretical accounts of ecological subjectivity are mired in a myriad of problems that stem from the attempt to somehow go back to a nature that pre-exists language and culture. Employing Lacanian theory, this paper aims to correct this misrecognition. It maps the putative ecological subject onto those fleeting moments of dislocation in which established discourses of nature and culture reveal their historically contingent origins.

Such a trend – which is the result of the residual filtering through of wider social changes, as well as dynamics peculiar to the psychoanalytic tradition itself – has, Carveth contends, robbed psychoanalysis of its central focus and contributed to the blunting of its personal and social efficacy, something which he naturally laments. Drawing heavily on the work of Eli Sagan, Carveth seeks to bring guilt back to the center of psychoanalytic theory and practice, and, at the same time, to provide psychoanalysis with a re-worked and clarified account of its own purpose and goal.

Trying to build a movement against ourselves? On reading Renee Lertzman’s Environmental melancholia: Psychoanalytic dimensions of engagement

Renee Lertzman Routledge, Hove, East Sussex; New York, NY, 2015, 240 pp., $111.97, ISBN-13: 978-0415727990

Matthew Adams

Matthew Adams

UK

Matthew Adams   a+44 01273 64451Matthew.adams@bton.ac.uk
climate change, environment, object relations, psychosocial, sustainability

This review essay reflects on Renee Lertzman’s Environmental Melancholia (2015), which understands human engagement with ongoing ecological crises as predominantly defined by loss, melancholy and ambivalence. The book provides a psychoanalytic and psychosocial analysis of engagement and non-engagement with environmental issues, based on in-depth interviews with respondents who live in close proximity to ‘ecologically beleaguered’ places. This review provides a brief overview of Lertzman’s rationale, methodology and analysis. It then offers some critical reflections on the dimensions of engagement Lertzman offers, in terms of her understanding of the nature of loss, the salience of unconscious dynamics and her utilisation of the psychosocial.

The call of character: Living a life worth living

Mari Ruti Columbia University Press, New York, 2013, pp. 224, hardcover, $27, ISBN-13: 978-0231164085

Tod Sloan

Tod Sloan

USA

Tod Sloan   asloan@lclark.edu

Translating complex theory into a meaningful, comprehensible form accessible to a wide range of readers is a challenge that Mari Ruti has regularly taken on and met over the course of her writing career, to which body of work The Call of Character is a compelling addition. The book explores core concepts from Nietzsche, Lacan, Heidegger, Badiou, Žižek, Butler, and Adorno to tackle puzzles such as desire, character, repetition, trauma, suffering, love, conformity, interpersonal ethics, creativity, and meaning-making. In so doing, Ruti’s psychoanalytically informed study explores ideas and processes that offer access to ways of enacting the aim she expresses in the work’s subtitle: Living a life worth living.

In the preface, Ruti encapsulates her organizing theme: living life well means fostering the expression of character. This entails being aware of our desire and honoring it as fully as possible in a deeply ethical manner. It also means opening to the possibilities presented by powerful events and encounters. Ruti encourages a form of self-surrender in order to enhance such processes of engagement as well as tap the meaningfulness of everyday experience. The body of the text explores related questions: What is meant by character and desire? How can character be expressed ethically? How does meaningfulness arise? What modes of relationship foster character? What types of authenticity and openness to experience nurture truthful and creative living?

The answers that unfold in The Call of Character follow the lines of an optimistic Lacanian vision that might be concisely articulated as follows: There exists something called desire. It is enigmatic, but “living well” means seeking both to know and express desire. Desire energizes us and does not fit easily into rational, religious, or conventional structures of action; nor can it be known directly, however. Nevertheless, it can be sensed, because it enlivens our experience, urging us repeatedly to move in specific directions and highlighting realms of our world with a particular aura that calls to us. Desire is also unruly and rebellious. It can puzzle us and make us anxious in ways that may incline us to fall back into conventionality.

Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies, object relations, psychoanalysis, cultural studies

This article explores the under-stated, shadowy but nevertheless significant role of psychoanalysis in the work of the Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies (CCCS) at Birmingham University in Britain, whose development it reviews from the latter’s inception in 1964. It notes an early distance between the emerging social and political focus of Cultural Studies, and what were perceived to be the individualist and liberal perspectives of Freudian psychoanalysis in Britain. It points out that psychoanalytic perspectives and methods came to have a significant role in its later writing, as the Centre engaged with issues of gender and race, complementing its earlier focus on social class. It was through the Lacanian rather than British object relations tradition that psychoanalytic ideas were first taken up and incorporated into the CCCS’s complex Gramscian analyses of cultures, ideologies and ‘conjunctures’. The idea is proposed that Stuart Hall’s and the CCCS’s conception of culture as a source of creativity and agency, as well as of repression, is, however, consistent with the approach to meaning and symbolism of the British analytic tradition, and that there is scope for a further conjunction of these approaches.

Élisabeth Roudinesco Translated by Gregory Elliott, London, Verso, 2014, 161 pp., $24.95, paper, ISBN: 978-1-78168-162-6

Derek Hook

USA

Derek Hook   a+1 412-396-6513hookd@duq.edu

On the face of it, Élisabeth Roudinesco’s new book is something of an oddity. Following the scholarly efforts that went into her previous texts on Lacan – particularly the formidable Jacques Lacan: An Outline of a Life and History of a System of Thought (1997) – her new text, Lacan: In Spite of Everything, cannot but amount to a modest undertaking. Motivated in part by a series of observations derived from the biographical research underpinning her previous work, it is, strictly speaking, an account not so much of Lacan, but of the task of researching him, and of the many frustrations the author encountered as part of this project (the lack of viable evidence about Lacan’s childhood, the inaccessibility of much of his surviving estate, the non-existence of a viable archive). The book is also a collection of reflections on how various of Lacan’s personal idiosyncrasies connect to facets of his thought. Hence, comments of the following sort:

Lacan was his own mother, his own father, his own progenitor, hence desirous of possessing things and beings. He loved lists, collections, unpublished texts and rare editions. This great theorist of the object relation, the necessity of lack, and promotion of the symbolic function of the father, spent his life thinking against himself – against his difficulty in being a father, against the anxiety of lack, against his detestation of mothers. (p. 12)

It is sometimes the case that scholars are only able to write with true economy and fluency about a given system of ideas once they have already scrutinized such a system at length elsewhere. One certainly has this impression in reading Roudinesco, who proves adept at producing such deft descriptions of key emblems in Lacan’s oeuvre, and linking them to crucial events in his own personal life. In the late 1930s, Lacan conducted an affair with Sylvia Bataille behind the back of his pregnant wife (both women were in fact pregnant at the same time) and kept his first offspring in the dark about the illegitimate sibling for more than 20 years. This, says Roudinesco, “was fertile ground on which he developed the theory of the Name-of-the-Father”, a concept which refers to

the signifier of the paternal role. Being the embodiment of the signifier because he calls the child by his name, the father intervenes with the child as depriver of the mother…the family is at the base of human societies solely because it is dominated by the primacy of language: naming, he argued, enables a subject to acquire an identity. (p. 36)

Martin Luther King Jr., Freddie Gray, Baltimore, psychoanalysis, urban uprising

This article looks to psychoanalytic theory to underscore how actions of collective refusal can disrupt systems of racial injustice. Specifically, I focus on the recent uprising in West Baltimore following the death of Freddie Gray, a black man killed while in police custody. I elaborate on Martin Luther King Jr.’s notion of “creative maladjustment” to reject the media’s depiction of the Baltimore uprising as indicative of pathology within the community and instead theorize the event as conducive to ethical and social change. Through King’s notion of “creative maladjustment” and a Lacanian notion of ethics, I contend that Baltimore dissidents have challenged the normalcy of structural racism, initiating a transformation in America’s approach to race-based dispossession, state violence, and mass incarceration.

Attachment research has demonstrated that stress related to the manner in which caregivers are present or absent may serve as a reliable index of an infant’s secure or insecure attachment style (Fonagy, 2001). It has also shown that an insecure attachment style is often indicative of a failed environmental provision. This insecure attachment style is characterized by a deep sense of estrangement and alienation that the self experiences in relation to others. In the book under review, Candida Yates explores how these dynamics that shape individual development likewise affect the structures of institutions, politics, and culture. Positing psychic alienation and insecurity as underlying the chaos of unregulated economies and financial mismanagement, Yates argues that radical psychic fragmentation exists at the very center of the discourses of harmony and prosperity espoused by neoliberal ideology. Through her thoughtful examination of these discourses, she suggests that lost care and estranged relationships are normative within the political sphere, and, moreover, that the resulting alienation produced by insecure attachment is belied in contemporary politics by a narrative of pseudo-intimacy.

Yates, a professor of culture and communication at Bournemouth University, makes eloquent use of British object relations theory, combined with a healthy dose of French critical theory and psychoanalysis, to analyze the erosion of what might be considered formerly forthright discourses within the political climate of Britain. Drawing upon object relations theory, Yates moves beyond well-worn Freudian-Marxist syntheses, offering a significantly different approach through an emphasis on subjective experience and feelings in relational contexts. Molly Hall

Molly Hall   amolly_hall@my.uri.edu

Literary trauma theorist Cathy Caruth’s most recent work, Listening to Trauma, does exactly that in each of the thirteen interviews Caruth thoughtfully conducts with leaders in the field of trauma work. The collection offer readers a chance to see familiar psychoanalytic practitioners and theorists in a new light, one that explores various ways of listening, illuminating different pathways towards recovery. Nowhere else in Caruth’s work, nor in trauma studies as it exists within the academy, has there been a work that attempts to perform the very ideas it theorizes by practicing them on its pages. Moreover, the text furthers the performative aspect of trauma studies by foregrounding the physicality of trauma, both as it is experienced by the sufferer and also in the practitioner’s treatment of it. Throughout these conversations, Caruth performs one of the central ideas discussed in the book, that is, the imperative of the analyst to co-create knowledge of the analysand’s experience of past trauma while at the same time maintaining the boundaries between analyst and analysand. As an extension of the contact-oriented space she foregrounds within theories of trauma treatment, Caruth makes explicit the materiality of trauma through an emphasis on trauma’s inscriptions on the body. This material aspect of trauma comes to the fore in interviews with several respected practitioners and theorists representing myriad fields including neurology, anthropology, literary criticism, and film, among others.

In her interviews, Caruth re-creates the analytic scene of listening. Caruth’s rapport with and attunement to the other allows for a dialectical emergence of knowledge, one that principally emanates from the interviewee, but is also shaped by Caruth’s comments and questions. Observing this practice, the reader gains critical insight into what it means to be a trauma scholar in one’s own field – actively engaged, even if s/he is not a practitioner in the clinical sense. For example, in Caruth’s interview with psychoanalyst Dori Laub, Laub explains that the analyst often functions as both witness and co-creator of the first external narrative of the traumatic event experienced by the patient. The challenge, as identified in Caruth’s interviews, is to find a way to meet the other where s/he stands without losing one’s self in the trauma narrative, overtaking it, or allowing it to overwhelm one’s self as analyst.

Dennis Foster

USA

Dennis Foster   adfoster@smu.edu

Given the title of their book, I suppose I shouldn’t be surprised that when Danielle Knafo and Rocco Lo Bosco look out on the world, they see perversion everywhere. The virtue of this focus is that their world, particularly in some of its more distressingly grotesque features, reveals an orderliness, an underlying orientation that helps make sense of ours. But the near universality of such perversion also tends to flatten that world. As they write at one point, “the fundamental course of perversion – the guarantee of its presence in human affairs – is the existential problem of being a conscious animal” (p. 158). We are human, and therefore perverse.

Knafo comes to this interest in the perverse in part through her clinical encounters with patients and their attachments to dolls. Part I focuses on three cases. The first, Jack, unable to form satisfying or lasting relationships with women, falls in love with a high-end silicone RealDoll, a life-like sex doll. Much as the stuffed animal in The Velveteen Rabbit is made real through love, Jack’s love makes the doll into a real woman, one who makes ordinary women almost unnecessary. We find out a lot from Knafo and Lo Bosco about the sex doll industry that Jack, like many others, comes to depend upon. Some young Japanese men, for example, are too busy for women; artists express themselves through dolls; frugal men find dolls cheaper than marriage; the fastidious find them to be cleaner (pp. 70–72). Apparently, most of us are a little pervy. Twice, Knafo lets us know that she was at first repulsed by Jack’s commitment to his doll, but then her “own perversity and a voyeuristic curiosity surfaced” (p. 63). Jack, however, went too far and, fearing “something might be wrong with him” (p. 71), sought Knafo’s help. The problem Jack and nearly everyone else suffers from, what opens them to perversion, is that they have been traumatized.

When questioned about his past, Jack’s memories came easily and with little resistance. He recalled that as a child he could do nothing right. His mother was an abusive woman whom he claimed enjoyed belittling him. She also relentlessly argued with her husband, whom she considered a loser. ‘You’re a carbon copy of your dad,’ she often told Jack. (pp. 73–74)

Who gets a fair go? A Žižekian reading of representations of asylum seekers in Australia

Chris McMillan

Chris McMillan

UK

Chris McMillan   About the Author Chris McMillan is a Lecturer in Sociology and Experiential Education at Arcadia University, London. amcmillanc@arcadia.edu
Slavoj Žižek, Australia, asylum seekers, ideological fantasy, universality

In this paper I seek to utilise a Žižekian reading of ideological fantasy, of universality and of the Real to examine Australian representations of asylum seekers. I argue that, whilst Žižek’s work is of value in identifying the political and fantasmatic logics of the field, particularly the grip of the ‘fair go’, his applied analysis of the ‘global order’ has limited potential in these geo-politically bounded circumstances. Conversely, Žižek’s understanding of universality does offer the conceptual tools to provide an alternative political practice that seeks to evoke those moments of impossibility within the Australian narrative of the fair go.

Psychoanalysis in a changing Cuba: A note from the field

David Strug

David Strug

USA

David Strug   astrug@yu.edu
Cuba, economic reform, psychoanalysis, psychotherapy, psychoanalytic association of Cuba (APDECU), socialism

In 2015 and 2016, the author and four other psychoanalysts from New York City visited Havana and met with the Psychoanalytic Association of Cuba (APDECU), a study group of the International Federation of Psychoanalytic Societies (IFPS). These meetings provided an important opportunity to learn about psychoanalysis in Cuba, a little known topic. The author discusses the APDECU’s history and its members’ interest in psychoanalysis, describes the trajectory of psychoanalysis since the Cuban Revolution of 1959, and observes how economic, political, and social change has affected this trajectory. Psychoanalytic private practice, as we know it in capitalist countries, ended with the revolution, and psychoanalytically-oriented clinicians are employed by state-run public health institutions. Cuba’s leaders have introduced unprecedented economic change since 2008, resulting in an increasing marketization and privatization of the economy, which they refer to as “updating” or “reforming” socialism. The author explores the impact that economic reform may have on the future development of psychoanalysis and on the professional identity of psychotherapists.

cultural studies, surveillance, CCTV, narcissism, fetishism, fantasy

Studies of surveillance and CCTV culture so far have strongly focused on the panoptical and ban-optical dimensions of the phenomena, stressing their authoritarian and socially divisive purposes and effects. This article argues for the need to also take into account the complicity and unconscious investment of the modern subject in forms of optical surveillance. Offering a series of psychoanalytically informed readings, it seeks to exemplify how cultural studies, as a discipline, will gain by (re)employing psychoanalytic approaches, and how it will be able, through addressing some of the unconscious motivations behind CCTV, to identify new possibilities for political interventions in surveillance practice.

Ross Truscott

Ross Truscott   atruscottross@gmail.com

The edited volume, Psychodynamic Psychotherapy in South Africa, is concerned primarily with how psychoanalytic practitioners located outside of institutionalized psychoanalysis encounter difference in post-apartheid South Africa. Against theoretical “purism,” the volume offers “a new hybrid theoretical framework which interrogates the assumptions of current psychoanalytic theory and expands its scope to include non-Western collectivist notions of self and community” (p. 273). I focus here on the various ways in which the chapters work within the twin assumptions that, first, apartheid arrested a capacity for empathy between those it inscribed as different and, second, that empathy is cardinal for a post-apartheid psychoanalysis that bridges historical differences. These assumptions will certainly resonate with a readership beyond South Africa. They are also, I want to suggest, worth worrying over.

In the opening chapter, Sally Swartz writes of the “deeply paranoid anxiety that kept white and black apart” (p. 17) during apartheid. Swartz’s framing of the problem in intersubjective terms is subtle and alert to the pitfalls of Kohutian empathy, though the restoration of empathy remains “an important prerequisite for fundamental transformation” (p. 17) that informs the itinerary of the psychotherapeutic process she plots from a lack of empathy towards its possibility. In her contribution, Yvette Esprey, too, attends to histories of racism that affect the analytic dyad. Esprey writes that an “impulse to other and to discriminate has the potential to interrupt the therapeutic endeavor, where the aim is to find a resonance of alikeness and therefore a vehicle to empathy” (p. 39). Like Swartz, the version of empathy affirmed by Esprey is one that leaves the empathic subject altered, their own subjectivity refigured in the encounter with another. Glenys Lobban takes up this motif in a personal narrative in which she becomes, quite literally, “hybridized” through tracing her own interracial family history; i.e. she does not simply identify with the other, but becomes – what was, for her, prior to this – other.

Psychoanalysis Culture & Society, neoliberalism, status of psychoanalysis, interdisciplinarity, unconscious dimensions of the social world

In this article we reflect on our time as editors of Psychoanalysis, Culture & Society. The article reviews some of the journal’s major contributions to psychoanalytic understanding of social and political problems; considers whether or not we are entering a post-neoliberal world; and discusses some of the challenges faced by PCS given the marginal status of psychoanalysis in the wider culture, the journal’s emphasis on interdisciplinarity, and its commitment to providing a space for multiple psychoanalytic voices. The article’s later sections consider some of the areas that remain underdeveloped in the journal’s coverage. In particular, the penultimate section explores the challenging task of specifying whether or not social entities, as opposed to individuals, can be said to have properties that are unconscious in the psychoanalytic sense.

This article discusses the use of an innovative research tool, the visual matrix (VM). The VM is a tool that uses the visual imagination, expressed both verbally and in drawing, to reveal hidden or unexpressed ideas, feelings and emotions in research subjects. It is hypothesised to be of particular utility in the study of psychologically painful and/or complex situations, where normal discourse cannot find a means of expression. This article focuses on a photograph of a little boy that was taken in 1944. Photographs, when viewed many years later, often bring back deep experiences, long past and somehow forgotten. Revisiting this photo 70 years later, the author began to experience it as an “evocative object” – that is, one with not merely a personal meaning, but a “social and cultural significance” as well (Bollas, 2009a, p.179). Associations to the photo brought back countless memories, which opened up wider social-historical dimensions. Using the concepts of collective memory and the associative unconscious, the author explores this single photograph to evoke the immense possibilities for new thinking that emerge from this medium.

Melanie Klein, postcolonial, race, reparation, coalition

Melanie Klein’s theory of psychic reparation has been rightly criticized for colonial assumptions about which objects and populations are deemed worthy of political reparation. Yet this article cautions against dismissing Klein’s account of reparation altogether, and advocates reading Klein against herself. Illustrating this argument, I offer an against-the-grain reading of the psychic dynamics of postcolonial conflict in another text widely criticized for its colonial assumptions: Star Trek. I focus on the anticolonial revolutionary character Kira Nerys in spinoff Deep Space Nine, who never forgives her colonial oppressors, but does integrate love and hate in the context of radical anticolonial coalition-building.

The Americanization of Narcissism

Elizabeth Lunbeck Harvard University Press, Cambridge, MA, 2014, pp. 384, $35.00 hardback, ISBN: 9780674724860

Narcissism and its Discontents

Julie Walsh Palgrave, Basingstoke, 2014, pp. 192, $95.00 hardback, ISBN: 978-1-137-33344-5

In a lecture to the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society of 5th March 1913, Freud emphasised that ‘narcissism has to remain for us an irreducible phenomenon, the basis of the libido theory’ (Nunberg and Federn, 1974, p. 175). Returning home from this lecture, Lou Andreas-Salomé wrote in her diary: ‘I had to give a lot of thought to these discussions insofar as they have to do with the concept of narcissism. It is certain that the concept is employed in two ways which could surely lead to extraordinarily disturbing misunderstandings’ (Andreas-Salomé, 1965, p. 109). In its first usage by Freud and his colleagues, the concept referred to a developmental stage in which the infant clings to a fantasy that it encompasses and enjoys sovereignty over the world, mistaking the support of the environment for personal omnipotence. In a second usage, however, the same term referred to the libidinal investment in the self as an object; such investment is not transitory, but the fundamental, creative and organising economy for self-other relations. Suggesting that Freud was aware of this troubling ambiguity in the concept, Andreas-Salomé reports that ‘Freud is perfectly right in speaking of it, as he does now, as a limiting concept, which serves as a receptacle for what remains unsolved and not a key to its solution…’ (p. 109). This is an extraordinary remark. In this perspective, the concept of narcissism would not offer a direct route through which the question of the meaning or organisation of the self could be solved. Instead, it would hold this question aloft, magnetising and holding together the concerns around this topic, thereby opening them for examination. Andreas-Salomé offers a beautiful image to capture this account. Just like Ovid’s Narcissus, gazing into the water and seeing his own projected and untouchable image, psychoanalysis would find a means of knowing the self through an illusionary image in the concept of narcissism.

superego, conscience, persecutory guilt, reparative guilt, borrowed guilt, capacity for concern

Freud’s decision to merge conscience into the superego has made it difficult to study conflict between them. While the superego comprises aggression turned back against the self, identification with the aggressor, and (often immoral) internalized social norms, conscience emerges from early libidinal attachments and identification with the nurturer. The distinction between superego and conscience is grounded in the Freudian and Kleinian distinctions between Thanatos and Eros and the paranoid-schizoid and depressive or reparative positions. While Freud, Alexander and Ferenczi all viewed the analytic cure as involving the demolition of the superego, mainstream psychoanalysis, following Strachey, has preferred superego modification to recognition of a separate conscience, failing to understand that it is only on the basis of conscience that one can know in which direction the superego needs to be modified. The social and cultural as well as the clinical import of these distinctions is explored.

Paul Hoggett

Paul Hoggett

Paul Hoggett   apaul.hoggett@uwe.ac.uk
performativity, quantification, the ideal, shame, populism

Organisational theorists use the term ‘performativity’ when examining how management maximises the efficiency of educated labour under neoliberalism. This essay will argue that performativity exploits the employee’s desire to achieve the ideal, yoking this to target setting and performance monitoring. Everything becomes quantified, including the self. Insecurity and failure lurk in the shadow of performativity and feelings of shame become pervasive, replacing guilt as an internal control mechanism. The paper will describe how the abject position of the self in the world of production finds some relief and compensation in the world of consumption where the self feels entitled to have what it wants and to have it now. The paper concludes by wondering whether, in countries like the US and the UK, neoliberalism’s new educated social classes have maintained their distinction from and dumped their shame upon the left-behind white working class, thereby reproducing the class divisions which currently fuel reactionary forms of populism.

From a common sense point of view, an ideology consists of a convergent set of ideas that promotes and pursues a single strategic cause. However, the argument of this paper is that ideology can be nourished by a seemingly divergent, even antagonistic, set of ideas. To support this argument, this paper refers to the post-revolutionary (1979) Iranian state where, in the face of a series of threatening external others, the theocratic political ideology of the state is complemented/supplemented by a return to an image of classical Persian identity. While the former identity is supported by the Shia value system, the latter draws its inspiration from Persian classical literature. To examine this situation, the current paper adopts a Lacanian perspective on the question of ideology, with a specific focus on the concepts of fantasy and jouissance as elaborated in the works of Lacanian political theorists.

In cultural studies, neoliberal capitalism has been critically discussed in connection with a rise of mental illness. Contemporary psychoanalysis is becoming increasingly attuned to the importance of multicultural and social justice concerns in clinical practice. However, the intersection of clinical and political praxis remains unclear in clinical theory. In order to address the split between theory and practice, Liberation Psychology, an influential movement in social justice and multicultural psychology, will be introduced through the work of Paulo Freire, who was in turn influenced by psychoanalytic insights. disgust, contempt, shame, humiliation, Trump

The election as president of the United States of an individual broadly perceived to be a threat to civil liberties has raised difficult questions about psychologists’ responsibilities for commenting on public affairs while concurrently retaining a respect for the rights of individuals to be spared undue personal scrutiny. While balancing these concerns, this paper examines a constellation of emotions that relate to self-regard maintenance in the face of interpersonal vulnerabilities. The emotions defined and discussed are disgust, contempt, shame, and humiliation. The author conjectures that Donald Trump’s relationship to this emotion constellation predicts the type of leadership he might provide as US president. His focus is on preserving elevated self-regard, and he is willing to pursue this aim through disidentification with many individuals and classes of people. This self-protective and self-elevating urge combines with Trump’s disregard for conventional morality around truthfulness and interpersonal restraint to create a readiness to disengage from the needs of large swathes of humanity.

Manuals for clinical practice arrive in numbers and in force, threatening the first of the particular with the first of a philosophy. Yet the individual with no manual but his/her own particularities is likely to suffer and make others suffer. Thus, respect for the quest to discover a manual coupled with persistence in rejecting all that come along seems a responsible course of action. If this struggle is embraced, it may generate a fecund state of mental tension, prone to surprises and sudden inspirations, which the writer calls dii-consciousness. Yet this manual must be discarded on the path, its truth no preservative against wilting.

Authoritarianism, reflective thinking, solidarity, manic defense, complementary relatedness

Self-reflective thinking guards against the flight to authoritarian fantasies and leaders—a flight seen recently, for example, in the election of Donald Trump as US president. The capacity to think reflectively requires a sense of security which, if not internalized, can come from a feeling of belonging. But, if we need to belong to feel secure, how free are we to think differently from the group? I propose two types of solidarity—true solidarity, where a sense of universal kinship fosters compassion and a sense of responsibility for care that makes it important to reflect on what we do; and false solidarity, a shared paranoid/manic fantasy of superiority to a despised group, in which personal thinking threatens a brittle sense of belonging. Right-wing populism is a way to cope with anxieties about economic/cultural dispossession through such fantasies of superiority. But the Left has its own false solidarity—a manic bond that refuses empathy with the pain of the dispossessed on the Right, and even attacks those on the Left who are deemed insufficiently attentive to particular social justice issues. False solidarity is likely to evoke a complementary reaction—similar aggressive, resistant attitudes—in those it targets, resulting in a political impasse. But humility and active compassion may open the way to real dialogue.

For those who have wrestled with the provocative and stimulating work of Slavoj Žižek, the publication of The Žižek Dictionary brings with it a sigh of relief. Žižek’s work has long called for a companion text able to shed light on his more obscure and challenging theorizations. There have been foreshadowings of such a text; introductions to the work of the Slovene philosopher have often included glossaries of technical and psychoanalytic terms deployed in his work. Yet given that many of these terms are derived from Lacanian theory, such glossaries have often slid into the uncertain territory of conflating Lacanian and Žižekian thought. Butler’s volume distinguishes itself in two essential respects: First, it represents the first stand-alone text devoted to defining key concepts essential to understanding Žižek’s theory. Second, it attends to the particularities that differentiate Žižek’s theorizations from Lacan’s. In these ways, Butler fills an important gap in Žižekian scholarship, and does so in erudite and often delightful ways.

The Žižek Dictionary, for a start, includes its fair share of wit. This is apparent not only in the fact that Žižek himself has contributed an entry – on, you guessed it, “Slavoj Žižek” – but also in Butler’s introduction to the volume, in which he speculates on “the Žižek transference effect.” Here, Butler includes an anecdote of his first meeting with the Slovene theoretician, who sat reading a book throughout a talk Butler was giving on Žižek himself. Such humor offers welcome relief from the mental labor that inevitably accompanies working through Žižekian thought.

This is not to suggest that the writing within the collection is unduly difficult. To be sure, Žižek’s theorizations are challenging; in response, the contributions as a whole are necessarily complex, while at the same time remaining largely accessible. A multi-authored text, The Žižek Dictionary, provides a diverse series of perspectives on Žižek’s work by some of the most promising contemporary Žižekian scholars, including Geoff Boucher on ideology, Glyn Daly on jouissance, Jodi Dean on law, Anthony Johnston on neuroscience, and Fabio Vighi on biopolitics. In Treatment, cultural studies, therapy, television, reflection

In recent years, critics working with psychoanalysis have increasingly turned their attention to the relationship between therapy and culture. Following Lacan and Foucault, many critics are wary of the way in which the idea of therapy has become a tool of surveillance and control, whilst those influenced by the object relations tradition concern themselves with the therapeutic effect that might be gleaned from cultural experience. Through a close reading of the HBO series In Treatment, this article explores the contours of this debate in order to theorise what psychoanalysis might offer to contemporary cultural studies. The article argues, ultimately, for a perspective informed by both Lacanian and object relations psychoanalysis that can account for the therapeutic value of cultural experience whilst concurrently offering a critical analysis of the ways in which representation is implicated in relations of power.

Mind zone: Therapists behind the front lines

Jan Haaken Herzog & Company, Los Angeles, CA, 2014

Neil Altman

Neil Altman

USA

Neil Altman   aaltman.neil@gmail.com

The traumatic stress faced by soldiers creates many still largely unresolved dilemmas for the governments that send troops to fight. Jan Haaken’s compelling documentary, Mind Zone: Therapists Behind the Front Lines, meaningfully addresses several of them through the lens of one central question: “Can a combat zone be turned into a mind zone?” A mind zone is a zone where mental processing can occur. In contemporary theory (e.g. Fonagy et al, 2002), “mentalization” refers to the sense of having a mind, or, in other words, a perspective on reality that is one’s own. Through mentalization, trauma can be transformed from an overwhelming shock felt as a dead weight upon the self to something that can be thought, an event about which one comes to possess one’s own individual perspective. Effective psychotherapeutic treatment of wartime trauma, then, like all that of all trauma, depends on enabling the patient’s capacity to think for him or herself. However, when psychotherapy is paid for by the Army and functionality is the goal, some forms of thinking for oneself, or even thinking at all, are likely to be seen as counter-productive.

This predicament is evidenced in the military’s need to train soldiers for unreflexive instantaneous action and the soldier’s need to feel that there exists some good reason for placing himself, often repeatedly, in a position to kill or be killed. If the therapist believes that psychological wellbeing depends on the kind of autonomy that entails a reflexive thoughtfulness about one’s actions, then there seems to exist an inherent conflict for the therapist between serving the patient and serving the “mission.” An additional complication for therapists is the fact that a soldier’s psychic health may be significantly impaired should he lack the ability to critically reflect upon the mission and return home to face potentially vehemently expressed opinions that the mission to which he has been committed was questionable or even futile, if not completely misguided.

Lacan, transgender, horror, castration, hysteria

In 2013, Russell Williams, a colonel in the Canadian military, pled guilty to eighty-eight violent charges, including two charges of sexual assault and two charges of first-degree murder. Drawing on narratives of (trans)gender anxiety popularized by horror films, the media built an explanatory framework which fixated upon Williams’ fetishistic cross-dressing. This article interrogates the site where fantasies of absolute sexed difference coincide with fantasies about military phallicism in the national psyche. Drawing on Lacan’s paternal metaphor, I argue that gender operates as a symptom, assuaging the anxiety that arises when a nation is confronted with the fallibility of sex binaries and phallic authority. The symbolic castration of Colonel Williams provides a case study of how the quest for a phallic master has cultivated a nation of hysterics.

This article analyzes Russia’s “conservative turn”, which occurred in 2012 when Vladimir Putin was elected President for a third time. An overview of this turn – incorporating anti-Westernism, an emphasis on tradition, the protection of symbols of purity, and the persecution of symbols of impurity – opens the article. The author then explains the concept of “perverse conservatism” and elaborates its basic pattern with reference to such Lacanian psychoanalytic concepts as subjectification, perversion, disavowal, and what he calls the “defensive fetish”. Finally, this pattern and its sub-patterns of fetishism and sadism are applied to an explanation of certain aspects of Russia’s domestic policy.
